title: Terminal Illness & End-of-Life Planning in Japan: 5-Step Official Checklist
titleEn: Terminal Illness & End-of-Life Planning in Japan: 5-Step Official Checklist
cardSummary: Official 5-step serious and terminal illness checklist for Japan: palliative care coordination, advance directives, powers of attorney, disability and caregiver support, and estate preparation.
introHtml: When a Japanese citizen living in Japan is facing a serious or life-limiting illness, putting medical, legal, and financial mandates in place while decision-making capacity remains intact prevents court delays and administrative uncertainty for your family member. Japanese law separates medical care discussions from formal property management, because ordinary agency rules and financial mandates require clear documentation, and statutory voluntary guardianship only takes effect after Family Court registration. This planning guide outlines official advance administration, healthcare, and benefit pathways based on Japanese government statutes and ministries [1][3][5].

steps.title: Healthcare access, palliative care, and hospital coordination
steps.html:
• National Health Insurance and high-cost medical caps: Verify active enrollment in National Health Insurance (Kokumin Kenko Hoken) or Employees' Health Insurance and apply for an Eligibility Certificate for Ceiling-Amount Application (Gendogaku Tekiyo Ninteisho) through the insurer or hospital social worker so monthly out-of-pocket medical bills are capped [1].
  • Long-Term Care Insurance assessment: Patients aged 65 or older (or aged 40 to 64 with designated terminal conditions such as terminal cancer) can apply through their municipal office for Long-Term Care Insurance (Kaigo Hoken) certification to cover home-visit nursing, care equipment, and palliative support [1][2].
  • Hospital medical social work teams: Coordinate early with the treating hospital's regional medical coordination and palliative care office so home hospice transitions, discharge equipment, and pain-management continuity are arranged seamlessly [1].

steps.title: Advance care planning and medical decision-making
steps.html:
• Jinsei Kaigi (Advance Care Planning) under MHLW guidance: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) promotes Jinsei Kaigi (Advance Care Planning), a structured, repeated discussion among your family member, loved ones, and the medical care team to document values and treatment preferences in the medical record [1].
  • Legal status of living wills in Japan: Japan has no standalone statute giving binding force to a standalone living will or medical power of attorney; documented wishes and designated spokesperson names guide clinical consensus under MHLW end-of-life decision guidelines rather than acting as self-executing legal orders [1].
  • Designated healthcare spokesperson: Record the name and contact details of one or more trusted people in hospital charts, confirm who may speak with doctors when the ill person cannot participate, and review written care preferences as conditions evolve [1].

steps.title: Financial mandates, powers of attorney, and voluntary guardianship
steps.html:
• Voluntary Guardianship Contract (Nin'i Koken Keiyaku): While full mental capacity remains, your family member can execute a Voluntary Guardianship Contract before a Japanese notary public (koshonin) under the Act on the Voluntary Guardianship Contract; the guardian gains authority once capacity declines and the Family Court appoints a Voluntary Guardianship Supervisor [5][6].
  • Bank mandates and guardianship registry: Japanese banks commonly restrict account access once incapacity is reported unless a registered guardian is appointed, so arrange immediate bill-payment delegations and review the Ministry of Justice (MOJ) Japan Adult Guardianship Registration System (Seinen Koken Toki) operated through Legal Affairs Bureaus [6][7].
  • Statutory guardianship fallback: If capacity is lost before a notarial Voluntary Guardianship Contract is signed, relatives must petition the Family Court for statutory Adult Guardianship, Curatorship, or Assistance under Book IV of the Civil Code, or consult the municipal support portal managed under Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) guidance [2][3].

steps.title: Disability pensions, caregiver leave, and financial support
steps.html:
• Disability Pension and Disability Allowance: Patients enrolled in the National Pension or Employees' Pension Insurance whose illness results in qualifying functional impairment may apply through Japan Pension Service (JPS) for the Disability Basic Pension (Shogai Kiso Nenkin), Disability Employees' Pension, or Disability Allowance after medical certification [8].
  • Sickness and Injury Allowance: Employed patients enrolled in Employees' Health Insurance who take unpaid medical leave due to illness can request Sickness and Injury Allowance (Shobyo Teatekin) from their health insurance association [1].
  • Family Care Leave (Kaigo Kyugyo) and subsidies: Under the Act on Childcare Leave, Caregiver Leave, and Other Measures for the Welfare of Workers Caring for Children or Other Family Members administered by Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW), eligible working caregivers may take up to 93 days of Family Care Leave (splittable into up to three separate periods per qualifying family member) alongside Employment Insurance Caregiver Leave Benefits [9].

steps.title: Wills, beneficiary records, and cross-border preparation
steps.html:
• Formal wills and Legal Affairs Bureau custody: Under Book V of the Civil Code and the Act on Storage of Wills in Legal Affairs Bureau administered by Ministry of Justice (MOJ) Japan, your family member can create either a Notarial Deed Will (kosei shosho yuigon) at a notary office or deposit a compliant handwritten holographic will at a Legal Affairs Bureau will storage office to eliminate post-death Family Court probate (kennin) and preserve safe custody [3][10][11].
  • Organize family register, property, and tax records: Compile current koseki records, real property title deeds (noting Japan's mandatory real property inheritance registration rules under Real Property Registration Act amendments effective 1 April 2024), insurance policies with named beneficiaries, and a full inventory of domestic and overseas accounts [4][12].
  • Apostille preparation for foreign assets: If records, powers, or certified identity documents will be used outside Japan, arrange notarization and free Hague Apostille certification through Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan (MOFA) (or One-Stop Service in Tokyo, Kanagawa, Osaka, or Fukuoka) while your family member can appear or instruct representatives directly [13].
